prompt: You raise the floor to 0.90. For the /search question, the best passage scores 0.86. What happens?

options.A: Only C2 passes, because a high floor removes near-duplicate passages such as C3
options.B: Every passage is dropped, so an answerable question gets “not in the docs”
options.C: Nothing changes, because the floor only applies to off-topic questions
options.D: The bot answers 10, because C3 is the one passage above the floor

prompt: Why keep a golden set instead of trying a few questions by hand after each change?

options.A: The similarity score already shows whether an answer is right, so hand checks add nothing
options.B: The same questions with known answers every run, so scores compare and regressions show
options.C: Hand checks rely on the LLM judge, which disagrees with human labels far too often
options.D: A golden set makes retrieval itself faster, because the right answers get cached

prompt: What does computing recall@k need?

options.A: For each question, which passage is right and where it ranked
options.B: An LLM judge scoring each answer against a written rubric
options.C: A person reading and grading every single answer the bot writes
options.D: The model's probability for every token of each answer

prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10” from C3, which really says 10. Is that answer faithful, and is it right?

options.A: Unfaithful and wrong: it changed the number given in the passage it read
options.B: Faithful but wrong: it stuck to its passage, but retrieval sent the wrong one
options.C: Faithful and right: it cited the passage it was given, so it is correct
options.D: Unfaithful but right: the model corrected a mistake in the passage

prompt: Your docs are 2M tokens and edited daily. Which approach fits?

options.A: RAG: about 1,000 input tokens per question, and edits show up once changed chunks are re-embedded
options.B: Raise k until it covers every chunk, because recall@k reaches 100% only when all chunks are sent
options.C: Fine-tuning: retrain daily, because the weights are the most reliable place to keep exact facts
options.D: Long context: paste everything, because a bigger prompt always gives the model more facts to use

prompt: Cosine similarity between a question and a passage measures…

options.A: How many exact words the question and the passage have in common
options.B: How likely the model is to generate the passage as its next text
options.C: How closely their embedding vectors point in the same direction
options.D: How long the passage is compared with the length of the question

prompt: Chunks of 6 words, no overlap: the chunk holding “100” reads “100 requests per minute per API”. Why is that a problem?

options.A: It breaks the index: chunks must share some words, or the index refuses to store them
options.B: It costs too much: small chunks send more tokens per question than large chunks do
options.C: It lost its subject: no chunk has /search with 100, so a /search question can't match it
options.D: It is too long: six words is more than one embedding vector can hold for retrieval

prompt: “How often can I call search per minute?” Which method on its own matches “call” to “requests”?

options.A: Vector search, because similar meanings get similar embeddings
options.B: Keyword search, because both words appear somewhere in the docs
options.C: Neither one, because only an LLM judge can match two synonyms
options.D: Keyword search, because rarer words count more in its scoring

prompt: Plain prompt, k = 1 → k = 3 on the golden set. Select all that are true.

options.A: G6's answer miss disappears
options.B: Retrieval misses drop from 3 to 0
options.C: End-to-end accuracy reaches 100%
options.D: Right answers rise from 2 to 5

prompt: Exact search over 100 million vectors of 1,024 numbers each. About how many multiply-adds per question, in billions?
“What does E1042 mean?” Vector search ranks the 429 passage first. Why does keyword search find C6?

options.A: Only C6 contains the exact token E1042, a rare word that keyword scoring rewards
options.B: Keyword search knows E1042 is an error code, so it ranks error passages first
options.C: Keyword search ranks passages by their length, and C6 is the shortest passage
options.D: Keyword search gives E1042 a longer vector, so its cosine with C6 comes out higher

prompt: With k = 1 the bot answered “10 requests per minute [C3]” to “How often can I call search per minute?”. Where was the bug?

options.A: The model: it ignored the passage it was given and answered from its training data instead
options.B: Generation: the model had C2 in its prompt but copied the wrong number out of that same passage
options.C: Chunking: C2 was split at a boundary, so the number 100 was missing from every chunk sent
options.D: Retrieval: C3 (/upload) ranked above C2, so the model answered faithfully from the wrong passage

prompt: The plain LLM judge passed “Limits vary by endpoint and plan; check your dashboard…”. What made it match the human label?

options.A: Switching to exact match, because exact match never passes long answers
options.B: Raising k, so that the judge sees more of the retrieved passages
options.C: A bigger judge model, because only small judges show verbosity bias
options.D: A rubric that says passing means stating 100 requests per minute for /search

prompt: Putting passage C2 in the prompt made “100” jump to 96%. What changed inside the model?

options.A: The weights updated to store the new fact, so later questions without C2 also answer 100
options.B: Nothing in the weights: attention read “100” from the passage now in the context
options.C: The vocabulary gained a token for 100, so the model could finally output it
options.D: Temperature dropped, because a passage in the prompt makes sampling greedy

prompt: G6: the right passage (24 hours) was retrieved, but the bot said 48 hours. What kind of miss, and what fixes it?

options.A: A grading miss: the judge misread an answer that was correct
options.B: A chunking miss: add overlap so the passage keeps its subject
options.C: An answer miss: fix the prompt or the model, since a bigger k can't help
options.D: A retrieval miss: raise k so that more of the ranked passages reach the prompt

prompt: In RAG, what does the generate stage actually receive?

options.A: The passages' embedding vectors, written into the model's weights for the length of one request
options.B: A prompt with instructions, the top k retrieved passages as text, and the question
options.C: The whole docs index, which the model searches itself during its forward pass
options.D: Only the question, because retrieval runs after generation to check the answer

prompt: Reference: “100 requests per minute per API key”. Why does exact match fail “100 requests per minute.”?

options.A: It compares strings, so a right answer worded differently fails
options.B: It fails any answer shorter than the reference, right or wrong
options.C: It applies the judge's rubric, which requires the words API key
options.D: It compares meanings, and the final period changes the meaning

prompt: What does half overlap between chunks fix?

options.A: Large chunks mix fewer topics, because overlap removes their repeated words
options.B: A fact cut at a chunk boundary also appears whole in the neighbouring chunk
options.C: Fewer chunks need storing, because overlapping chunks are merged into one
options.D: The question and the chunks can now use two different embedding models

prompt: Today: vector search, k = 3, recall 100%, 1,000 tokens per question. Gate: recall ≥ today and tokens ≤ today. Which change ships?

options.A: Hybrid search with k = 1: recall 83% with 400 tokens
options.B: Hybrid search with k = 2: recall 100% with 700 tokens
options.C: Vector search with k = 2: recall 83% with 700 tokens
options.D: Vector search with k = 4: recall 100% with 1,300 tokens

prompt: You paste 50,000 tokens of docs into every question, at $3 per million input tokens. What does one question cost, in dollars?
Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add facts the bot must quote exactly?

options.A: Fine-tuning only changes the tokenizer, so the new facts never reach the weights
options.B: A fine-tuned model needs a longer context window for every question it is asked
options.C: Fine-tuning erases the model's earlier training, so it forgets how to write sentences
options.D: Each edit needs a training run, and the model can't point to where a fact came from

prompt: Right-passage ranks for six golden questions are 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 1. What is recall@2, in percent?
Your docs are 50K tokens and change rarely. The context window is 128K. What's the simplest good choice?

options.A: Paste all the docs into the prompt; prompt caching cuts the repeated cost
options.B: Fine-tune on the docs, because facts in the weights cost no input tokens
options.C: Build RAG, because a long prompt can never show which passage it used
options.D: None works, because 50K tokens is over the model's context window limit

prompt: Why must the question and the chunks go through the same embedding model?

options.A: The context window only accepts vectors made by the model that writes the answer
options.B: Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces, so their cosine means nothing
options.C: Keyword scores are computed from the embedding model's vocabulary of rare words
options.D: Different models cut the docs into different chunks, so their ranks can't be compared

prompt: In vector search, what is embedded ahead of time, and what at ask time?

options.A: Nothing ahead of time; the model embeds the docs during its prefill
options.B: Both at ask time, because each chunk's vector depends on the question
options.C: The question ahead of time; every chunk at ask time, to stay fresh
options.D: Every chunk ahead of time (the index); the question at ask time

prompt: An approximate index checks only the regions nearest the question. What does it give up for the speed?

options.A: Precision: the cosine scores it returns are rounded, so ties appear
options.B: Cost: every approximate search adds extra input tokens to the prompt
options.C: Freshness: a newly added vector can't be found until the next full rebuild
options.D: Recall: a true nearest neighbour in an unchecked region can be missed

prompt: Hybrid search raises recall@1 from 50% to 83%. Why still read the per-question list?

prompt: You ask a model, with no docs in the prompt, for your API's /search limit (100 per minute, written only in your private docs). What does it most likely do?
